[![Donald Trump and Xi Jinping stand next to each other, both wearing suits](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/Donald_Trump_visit_to_China%2C_May_2026_P20260514DT-1642.jpg/250px-Donald_Trump_visit_to_China%2C_May_2026_P20260514DT-1642.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Donald_Trump_visit_to_China,_May_2026_P20260514DT-1642.jpg)

President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") with Chinese leader [Xi Jinping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping") during his [state visit to China in 2026](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_state_visit_by_Donald_Trump_to_China "2026 state visit by Donald Trump to China")

The relationship between the [People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Republic_of_China "People's Republic of China") (PRC) and the [United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States "United States") (US) has been complex and at times tense since the [establishment of the PRC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proclamation_of_the_People's_Republic_of_China "Proclamation of the People's Republic of China") on 1 October 1949 and subsequent [retreat of the government of the Republic of China to Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuomintang's_retreat_to_Taiwan "Kuomintang's retreat to Taiwan"). After the normalization of relations in the 1970s, the US–China relationship has been marked by persistent disputes including China's economic policies, the [political status of Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Political_status_of_Taiwan "Political status of Taiwan") and [territorial disputes in the South China Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Territorial_disputes_in_the_South_China_Sea "Territorial disputes in the South China Sea"). Despite these tensions, the two nations have significant economic ties and are deeply interconnected, while also engaging in [strategic competition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Strategic_competition "Strategic competition") on the global stage. As of 2025, the US and China are the world's [largest and second-largest economies by nominal GDP](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_GDP_(nominal) "List of countries by GDP (nominal)"). Collectively, they account for 44.2% of the global nominal GDP.

The proclamation of the PRC in Beijing by the [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") (CCP) chairman [Mao Zedong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mao_Zedong "Mao Zedong") created a new [central government](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_People's_Government_of_the_People's_Republic_of_China_(1949%E2%80%931954) "Central People's Government of the People's Republic of China (1949–1954)") on the [mainland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_China "Mainland China") in October 1949. Relations between the US and the new Chinese government quickly soured, culminating in direct conflict during the [Korean War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Korean_War "Korean War"). The US-led [United Nations intervention](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Command "United Nations Command") was met with [Chinese military involvement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_in_the_Korean_War "China in the Korean War"), as China sent millions of soldiers to prevent a US-aligned presence on its border. For decades, the US did not formally recognize the PRC, instead maintaining diplomatic relations with the [Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China "Republic of China") (ROC) based in Taiwan, and as such blocked the PRC's entry into the United Nations. However, shifting geopolitical dynamics, including the [Sino-Soviet split](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sino-Soviet_split "Sino-Soviet split"), the winding down of the [Vietnam War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War "Vietnam War"), as well as of the [Cultural Revolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cultural_Revolution "Cultural Revolution"), paved the way for US president [Richard Nixon's 1972 visit to China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_visit_by_Richard_Nixon_to_China "1972 visit by Richard Nixon to China"), ultimately marking a sea change in US–China relations. On 1 January 1979, the US formally established diplomatic relations with the PRC and recognized it as the sole legitimate [government of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_China "Government of China"), while maintaining unofficial ties with Taiwan via the [Taiwan Relations Act](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan_Relations_Act "Taiwan Relations Act"), which endures as a major point of contention.

Every US president since Nixon has toured China during his term in office, with the exception of [Jimmy Carter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jimmy_Carter "Jimmy Carter") and [Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joe_Biden "Joe Biden"). The two countries cooperated with each other against the Soviet Union. Following China's [reform and opening up](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reform_and_opening_up "Reform and opening up"), the trade between the two countries significantly increased starting from the 1980s, and the US gave China the [most favored nation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Most_favoured_nation "Most favoured nation") designation in 2001. The [Obama administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Barack_Obama "Presidency of Barack Obama") signed a record number of bilateral agreements with China, particularly regarding climate change, though its [Pivot to Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Asian_foreign_policy_of_the_Obama_administration "East Asian foreign policy of the Obama administration") created diplomatic friction.

Relations worsened during the 2010s over concerns including China's [militarization of the South China Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Territorial_disputes_in_the_South_China_Sea#Chinese_policies "Territorial disputes in the South China Sea") and [Chinese espionage in the United States](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_espionage_in_the_United_States "Chinese espionage in the United States"),[[1]](#cite_note-bbc._WhyU-1)[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-3) leading observers to speculate a [Second Cold War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Cold_War#Usage_in_the_context_of_China%E2%80%93United_States_tensions "Second Cold War") between the two powers.[[4]](#cite_note-4)[[5]](#cite_note-5) In 2018, President [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") launched a [trade war with China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China%E2%80%93United_States_trade_war "China–United States trade war"). The relationship further deteriorated during the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic"). In January 2021, the US officially classified the Chinese government's treatment of the [Uyghurs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uyghurs "Uyghurs") in Xinjiang [as a genocide](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persecution_of_Uyghurs_in_China#Genocide "Persecution of Uyghurs in China").[[6]](#cite_note-Bernstein-2021-6) Tensions remained high during the [presidency of Joe Biden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Presidency_of_Joe_Biden "Presidency of Joe Biden") from 2021. [His foreign policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_policy_of_the_Biden_administration#China "Foreign policy of the Biden administration") prioritized strategic competition with China,[[7]](#cite_note-7)[[8]](#cite_note-8) imposed [export controls on semiconductors to China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_New_Export_Controls_on_Advanced_Computing_and_Semiconductors_to_China "United States New Export Controls on Advanced Computing and Semiconductors to China"),[[9]](#cite_note-9) boosted regional alliances against China, and expanded support for Taiwan.[[10]](#cite_note-Lau-2021-10)[[11]](#cite_note-11) However, the administration also emphasized that the US sought "competition, not conflict".[[12]](#cite_note-12) The [second Trump administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_presidency_of_Donald_Trump "Second presidency of Donald Trump")'s relations with China has been marked by inconsistency. From 2025, the administration sharply escalated the trade war with China, [raising tariffs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tariffs_in_the_second_Trump_administration "Tariffs in the second Trump administration"), prior to negotiating with China on a reduction in the tariff rate. Trump administration has emphasized economic competition over ideological conflicts.

The [People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") (PRC) was founded on 1 October 1949.

On 25 June 1950, the China-aligned state of [North Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Korea "North Korea") invaded US-aligned [South Korea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Korea "South Korea").[[13]](#cite_note-Chen-1992-13) In response, the [United Nations Security Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_Security_Council "United Nations Security Council") passed [Resolution 82](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Na

The [Prime Minister of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_India "Prime Minister of India"), [Narendra Modi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narendra_Modi "Narendra Modi") meeting the [Chinese leader](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paramount_leader "Paramount leader"), [Xi Jinping](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xi_Jinping "Xi Jinping"), in [Wuhan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wuhan "Wuhan"), China during a [Shanghai Cooperation Organisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_Cooperation_Organisation "Shanghai Cooperation Organisation") [summit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_Tianjin_SCO_summit "2025 Tianjin SCO summit") on 31 August 2025

[China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China "China") and [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India "India") maintained peaceful relations for thousands of years, but their relationship has varied since the [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") (CCP)'s victory in the [Chinese Civil War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Civil_War "Chinese Civil War") in 1949 and the [annexation of Tibet by the People's Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annexation_of_Tibet_by_the_People's_Republic_of_China "Annexation of Tibet by the People's Republic of China"). The two nations have sought economic cooperation with each other, while frequent border disputes and [economic nationalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_nationalism "Economic nationalism") in both countries are major points of contention.

Cultural and economic relations between China and India date back to ancient times. The [Silk Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk_Road "Silk Road") not only served as a major [trade route](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_route "Trade route") between India and China, but is also credited for facilitating the spread of [Buddhism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhism "Buddhism") from India to East Asia.[[1]](#cite_note-Maria-1) During the 19th century, the British [East India Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_India_Company "East India Company") increasingly [exported opium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opium_trade_in_China "Opium trade in China"), grown in India, leading to the [Opium Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opium_Wars "Opium Wars").[[2]](#cite_note-2)[[3]](#cite_note-Sen2003-3) During [World War II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II "World War II"), both [British India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Raj "British Raj") and the [Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China_(1912%E2%80%931949) "Republic of China (1912–1949)") (ROC) played a crucial role in halting the progress of [Imperial Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperial_Japan "Imperial Japan").[[4]](#cite_note-Barbara-4) After India became independent in 1947, it established relations with the ROC. The modern Sino-Indian diplomatic relationship began in 1950, when India was among the first noncommunist countries to end formal relations with the [Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China "Republic of China") and recognise the PRC as the legitimate government of both [Mainland China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_China "Mainland China") and [Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geography_of_Taiwan "Geography of Taiwan"). China and India are two of the major [regional powers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regional_power "Regional power") in Asia, and are the two [most populous countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_population "List of countries by population") and among the [fastest growing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_real_GDP_growth_rate "List of countries by real GDP growth rate") major economies in the world.

Growth in diplomatic and economic influence has increased the significance of their bilateral relationship. Between 2008 and 2021, China was India's largest trading partner, and the two countries have extended their strategic and military relations.[[5]](#cite_note-5)[[6]](#cite_note-6)[[7]](#cite_note-Hindu1-7)[[8]](#cite_note-NDTV-8) India has a large [trade deficit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trade_deficit "Trade deficit") that is favoured towards China. The [Sino-Indian border dispute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sino-Indian_border_dispute "Sino-Indian border dispute"), manifested by the [Line of Actual Control](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Line_of_Actual_Control "Line of Actual Control") (LAC), remains a central issue, resulting in the 1962 [Sino-Indian War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sino-Indian_War "Sino-Indian War"), the [clashes in 1967](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathu_La_and_Cho_La_clashes "Nathu La and Cho La clashes"), and the [a standoff in 1987](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1987_Sino-Indian_skirmish "1987 Sino-Indian skirmish").[[9]](#cite_note-APCSS-9) Since the late 1980s, both countries have rebuilt diplomatic and economic ties; a 1996 agreement forbids firearms and explosives near the LAC.[[10]](#cite_note-10)

Border deconfliction mechanisms emerged, beginning with the 2003 [Special Representatives](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Representative_mechanism_on_the_India%E2%80%93China_boundary_question "Special Representative mechanism on the India–China boundary question"). Renewed conflicts included [standoffs in 2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Depsang_standoff "2013 Depsang standoff"), and [in 2017](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_China%E2%80%93India_border_standoff "2017 China–India border standoff"); [major skirmishes in 2020-2021](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020%E2%80%932021_China%E2%80%93India_skirmishes "2020–2021 China–India skirmishes") resulted in dozens of deaths on both sides; military infrastructure near the LAC continues to grow.[[11]](#cite_note-WSJ-11)[[12]](#cite_note-12) India's concerns include China's [close relations with Pakistan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China%E2%80%93Pakistan_relations "China–Pakistan relations"),[[13]](#cite_note-13) and with [separatist groups in Northeast India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Insurgency_in_Northeast_India "Insurgency in Northeast India").[[14]](#cite_note-14) China's concerns include Indian military and economic activities in the disputed [South China Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_China_Sea "South China Sea")[[15]](#cite_note-15) and hosting of [Tibetan exiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibetan_exile "Tibetan exile").[[16]](#cite_note-16)[[17]](#cite_note-17) Today, South Asia is the primary site of [great power competition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_power_competition "Great power competition") between China and Ind

[Xiangqi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xiangqi "Xiangqi"), or Chinese chess, which, like [Western Chess](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chess "Chess") is believed to be descended from the Indian chess game of [chaturanga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chaturanga "Chaturanga").[[23]](#cite_note-23) The earliest indications reveal the game may have been played as early as the third century BCE.

China and India have also had some contact before the transmission of Buddhism. References to a people called the *[Chinas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinas "Chinas")*, are found in ancient [Indian literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_literature "Indian literature"). The [Indian epic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_epic_poetry "Indian epic poetry") *[Mahabharata](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahabharata "Mahabharata")* (c. 5th century BCE) contains references to "[China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/China_in_the_Mah%C4%81bh%C4%81rata "China in the Mahābhārata")", which may have been referring to the [Qin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qin_(state) "Qin (state)") state which later became the [Qin dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qin_dynasty "Qin dynasty"). [Chanakya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chanakya "Chanakya") (c. 350–283 BCE), the prime minister of the [Maurya Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurya_Empire "Maurya Empire"), refers to Chinese silk as "cinamsuka" (Chinese silk dress) and "cinapatta" (Chinese silk bundle) in his *[Arthashastra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arthashastra "Arthashastra")*.[[24]](#cite_note-24)

[Buddhism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buddhism "Buddhism") was transmitted from India to China in the 1st century CE.[[25]](#cite_note-25) Trade relations via the [Silk Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk_Road "Silk Road") acted as economic contact between the two regions.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*]

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/af/Ambassador_from_Zhong_Tianzhu_%28%E4%B8%AD%E5%A4%A9%E7%AB%BA_Central_India%29_in_The_Gathering_of_Kings_%28%E7%8E%8B%E4%BC%9A%E5%9B%BE%29_circa_650_CE.jpg/250px-Ambassador_from_Zhong_Tianzhu_%28%E4%B8%AD%E5%A4%A9%E7%AB%BA_Central_India%29_in_The_Gathering_of_Kings_%28%E7%8E%8B%E4%BC%9A%E5%9B%BE%29_circa_650_CE.jpg)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Ambassador_from_Zhong_Tianzhu_(%E4%B8%AD%E5%A4%A9%E7%AB%BA_Central_India)_in_The_Gathering_of_Kings_(%E7%8E%8B%E4%BC%9A%E5%9B%BE)_circa_650_CE.jpg)

Ambassador from Central India (中天竺 *Zhong Tianzhu*) to the court of the [Tang dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tang_dynasty "Tang dynasty"). *Wanghuitu* (王会图) circa 650 CE.

From the 1st century onwards, many Indian scholars and monks traveled to China, such as [Batuo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batuo "Batuo") ([fl.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floruit "Floruit") 464–495 CE)—first abbot of the [Shaolin Monastery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaolin_Monastery "Shaolin Monastery")—and [Bodhidharma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bodhidharma "Bodhidharma")—founder of [Chan/Zen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zen "Zen") Buddhism—while many Chinese scholars and monks also traveled to India, such as [Xuanzang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xuanzang "Xuanzang") (b. 604) and [I Ching](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Ching_(monk) "I Ching (monk)") (635–713), both of whom were students at [Nalanda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nalanda "Nalanda") University in [Bihar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bihar "Bihar").

#### Tang and Harsha dynasties

[[edit](/w/index.php?title=China%E2%80%93India_relations&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Tang and Harsha dynasties")]

During the 7th century, [Tang dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tang_dynasty "Tang dynasty") China gained control over large portions of the [Silk Road](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk_Road "Silk Road") and Central Asia. In 649, the Chinese general [Wang Xuance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Xuance "Wang Xuance"), along with thousands of recruited Tibetan and Nepalese troops, briefly invaded North India and won the [Battle of Chabuheluo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Chabuheluo "Battle of Chabuheluo").

During the 8th century, the astronomical [table](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aryabhata's_sine_table "Aryabhata's sine table") of [sines](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trigonometric_functions "Trigonometric functions") by the [Indian astronomer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_astronomy "Indian astronomy") and [mathematician](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_mathematics "Indian mathematics"), [Aryabhatta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aryabhatta "Aryabhatta") (476–550), were translated into the [Chinese astronomical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_astronomy "Chinese astronomy") and [mathematical](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_mathematics "Chinese mathematics") book of the *[Treatise on Astrology of the Kaiyuan Era](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Treatise_on_Astrology_of_the_Kaiyuan_Era "Treatise on Astrology of the Kaiyuan Era")* (*Kaiyuan Zhanjing*), compiled in 718 CE during the Tang dynasty.[[26]](#cite_note-needham_volume_3_109-26) The *Kaiyuan Zhanjing* was compiled by [Gautama Siddha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gautama_Siddha "Gautama Siddha"), an astronomer and astrologer born in Chang'an, and whose family was originally from India. He was also notable for his translation of the [Navagraha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Navagraha "Navagraha") calendar into Chinese.

Tamil Hindu Indian merchants traded in [Quanzhou](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quanzhou "Quanzhou") during the Yuan dynasty.[[27]](#cite_note-27)[[28]](#cite_note-28)[[29]](#cite_note-29) Hindu statues were found in Quanzhou dating to this period.[[30]](#cite_note-30)

According to [Badauni](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Badauni "Badauni") and [Ferishta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Firishta "Firishta"), the [Delhi Sultanate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi_Sultanate "Delhi Sultanate") under [Muhammad bin Tughluq](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_bin_Tughluq "Muhammad bin Tughluq") had ambitions to invade China. There existed a direct trade relationship between China and the Delhi Sultanate. Ibn Battuta mentions that the [Yuan Emperor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuan_dynasty "Yuan dynasty") had sent an embassy to Muhammad for reconstruction of a sacked temple at [Sambhal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sambhal "Sambhal").

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/74/Treasure_Boat_Shipyard_-_stele_pavilion_-_Calicut_stele_-_P1080100.JPG/250px-Treasure_Boat_Shipyard_-_stele_pavilion_-_Calicut_stele_-_P1080100.JPG)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Treasure_Boat_Shipyard_-_stele_pavilion_-_Calicut_stele_-_P1080100.JPG)

[Stele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stele "Stele") installed in [Calicut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kozhikode "Kozhikode") by [Zheng He](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zheng_He "Zheng He") (modern replica)

Between 1405 and 1433, [Ming dynasty](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ming_dynasty "Ming dynasty") China sponsored a [series of seven naval expeditions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ming_treasure_voyages "Ming treasure voyages") led by Admiral [Zheng He](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zheng_He "Zheng He"). Zheng He visited numerous Indian kingdoms and ports, including the [Malabar coast](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malabar_coast "Malabar coast"), [Bengal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bengal "Bengal"), and [Ceylon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceylon "Ceylon"), the [Persian Gulf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Persian_Gulf "Persian Gulf"), [Arabia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabia "Arabia"), and later expeditions ventured down as far as [Malindi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malindi "Malindi") in what is now [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya"). Throughout his travels, Zheng He liberally dispensed Chinese gifts of silk, [porcelain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Porcelain "Porcelain"), and other goods. In return, he received rich and unusual presents, including African zebras and giraffes.[[31]](#cite_note-31) After the Ming treasure voyages, private Chinese traders continued operating in the eastern Indian Ocean. Chinese junks could frequently be seen in the ports of the [Vijayanagara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vijayanagara "Vijayanagara") Empire, carrying silks and other products.[[32]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTENilakanta_Sastri2002304–305-32)

The [Bhois](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bhoi_dynasty "Bhoi dynasty") of [Orissa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Odisha "Odisha") maintained minor maritime trade links with China. Many of the [gosains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gosains "Gosains") entering Tibet from China passed through the territory of Birakisore Deva I of Khurda (1736–1793) who styled himself as Gajapati, the ruler of Utkala, when visiting the Jagannath temple at Puri.[[33]](#cite_note-33)

The reign of [Tipu Sultan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tipu_Sultan "Tipu Sultan") in [Mysore](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Mysore "Kingdom of Mysore") saw Chinese technology used for sugar production,[[34]](#cite_note-seri2-34) and sandalwood was exported to China.[[35]](#cite_note-sandal-35) Tipu's and Mysore's tryst with silk began in the early 1780s when he received a silk cloth from an ambassador from the Qing dynasty-ruled China at his court. Tipu was said to be enchanted by the item to such an extent that he resolved to introduce its production in his kingdom. He sent a return journey to China, which returned after twelve years.[[36]](#cite_note-36)

estern imperialism") in exchange for China's support for [Indian independence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_independence_movement "Indian independence movement"), the Chiangs visited [British India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_India "British India") in 1942 and met with Nehru, [Mahatma Gandhi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahatma_Gandhi "Mahatma Gandhi"), and [Muhammad Ali Jinnah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muhammad_Ali_Jinnah "Muhammad Ali Jinnah"). The Chiangs also sought to present their nation as a potential third option for the Indian people to ally themselves with, with public sympathies at the time sharply split between the British and the Japanese, who actively tried to sway India's population with pledges to liberate Asia if they would help their efforts against the British. While the public reception to the Chiangs was mostly positive, some reacted less favorably to the Chiangs' presence in India, with Jinnah believing that Chiang Kai-shek lacked proper understanding of Indian society and feeling he was biased in favor of Nehru and Gandhi while neglecting the demands of other religious communities.[[49]](#cite_note-49) For his part, Chiang apparently believed none of the major Indian leaders could help his government meaningfully. Nevertheless, the Chiangs continued to commit themselves to supporting the [Indian independence movement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_independence_movement "Indian independence movement") from afar, mostly via diplomacy, with Song Meiling writing to Nehru encouragingly: "We shall leave nothing undone in assisting you to gain freedom and independence."[[50]](#cite_note-50)

In 1942, a division of the [Kuomintang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kuomintang "Kuomintang")'s armies entered India as the [Chinese Army in India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Army_in_India "Chinese Army in India") in their struggle against Japanese expansion in [Southeast Asia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Asia "Southeast Asia").[[51]](#cite_note-51)[[52]](#cite_note-52)

On 15 August 1947, India gained independence from the United Kingdom. The newly independent India established diplomatic relations with the ROC. On 1 October 1949, the Chinese [People's Liberation Army](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People's_Liberation_Army "People's Liberation Army") defeated the Kuomintang (the ROC's ruling Nationalist Party) and took over [Mainland China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mainland_China "Mainland China"), establishing the PRC. Soon afterwards, India became a federal, democratic republic after its constitution came into effect on 26 January 1950.

> Their last telegrame to us is an act of gross discourtesy [...] It looks as though it is not a friend speaking in that language but a potential enemy [...] for the first time, after centuries, India’s defence has to concentrate itself on two fronts simultaneously. [...] In our calculations we shall now have to reckon with communist China in the north and in the north-east, a communist China which has definite ambitions and aims and which does not, in any way, seem friendly disposed towards us.

— Excerpt from Home Minister [Sardar Patel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vallabhbhai_Patel "Vallabhbhai Patel")'s letter to Prime Minister Jawaharlal Nehru, November 7, 1950[[53]](#cite_note-53)

India [established diplomatic relations with the PRC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dates_of_establishment_of_diplomatic_relations_with_the_People's_Republic_of_China "Dates of establishment of diplomatic relations with the People's Republic of China") on 1 April 1950, the first non-communist/socialist nation in Asia to do so.[[54]](#cite_note-54) Pakistan continued to recognize the ROC until 1951.[[55]](#cite_note-55)

The relationship between India and a newly communist China started out on an optimistic note. Jawaharlal Nehru, the first prime minister of India, and [PRC premier](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Premier_of_China "Premier of China") [Zhou Enlai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zhou_Enlai "Zhou Enlai") articulated a vision of an internationalist foreign policy governed by the ethics of the Panchsheel ([Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Principles_of_Peaceful_Coexistence "Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence")).[[56]](#cite_note-56) However, there was notable skepticism on the Indian side from the very beginning about Chinese intentions. For example, [Bhimrao Ambedkar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/B._R._Ambedkar "B. R. Ambedkar") was surprised that Nehru took Panchsheel seriously,[[57]](#cite_note-LL_Mehrotra-57) while [Acharya Kriplani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Acharya_Kriplani "Acharya Kriplani") said that Panchsheel was "born in sin".[[57]](#cite_note-LL_Mehrotra-57) Nehru himself was disappointed when it became clear that the two countries had a conflict of interest in Tibet, which had traditionally served as a [buffer zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buffer_zone "Buffer zone").[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] From the Chinese side, strategists were concerned about the possibility of India continuing to spread its dominance in Asia and the Indian Ocean in the manner of British India.[[58]](#cite_note-58)

China viewed Tibet as a part of its territory. The preceding government of the [Republic of China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Republic_of_China_(1912%E2%80%931949) "Republic of China (1912–1949)") under [Chiang Kai-shek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiang_Kai-shek "Chiang Kai-shek") also [claimed Tibet as Chinese territory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibet_Area_(administrative_division) "Tibet Area (administrative division)"). However, he was unable to re-assert control. [Chairman of the Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chairman_of_the_Chinese_Communist_Party "Chairman of the Chinese Communist Party") [Mao Zedong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mao_Zedong "Mao Zedong") saw Indian concern over Tibet as a manifestation of interference in the internal affairs of the PRC. The PRC reasserted control over Tibet and to end [Tibetan Buddhism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tibetan_Buddhism "Tibetan Buddhism") and [feudalism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Feudalism "Feudalism"), which it did by force of arms in 1950.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] To avoid antagonizing the PRC, Nehru informed Chinese leaders that India had no political ambitions or territorial ambitions and did not seek special privileges in Tibet, but that traditional trading rights must continue.[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] With Indian support, Tibetan delegates signed an agreement in May 1951 recognizing PRC sovereignty[*[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")*] but guaranteeing that the existing political and social system of Tibet would continue.

Chairman [Mao Zedong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mao_Zedong "Mao Zedong") of the [Chinese Communist Party](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_Communist_Party "Chinese Communist Party") and [Prime Minister](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_Minister_of_India "Prime Minister of India") Jawaharlal Nehru.
In April 1954, India and the PRC signed an eight-year agreement on Tibet that became the [Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Principles_of_Peaceful_Coexistence "Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence") (or *Panchsheel*). [Jawaharlal Nehru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jawaharlal_Nehru "Jawaharlal Nehru") of India, during the [latter's state visit to China](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Five_Principles_of_Peaceful_Coexistence "Five Principles of Peaceful Coexistence"), October 1954.

In October 1954, China and India signed an [agreement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sino-Indian_Agreement_1954 "Sino-Indian Agreement 1954") regarding Tibet, whereby India recognised Tibet as part of China, with China accepting the continuance of the previous trade arrangements. Observers noted the agreement heavily favored China.[[59]](#cite_note-59)

It is the popular perception that the catchphrase of India's diplomacy with China in the 1950s was *Hindi-Chini bhai-bhai*, which means, in [Hindi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindi "Hindi"), "Indians and Chinese are brothers".[[60]](#cite_note-60) Nehru sought to initiate a more direct dialogue between the peoples of China and India in culture and literature. Around then, the Indian artist (painter) [Beohar Rammanohar Sinha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beohar_Rammanohar_Sinha "Beohar Rammanohar Sinha"), who had earlier decorated the pages of the original [Constitution of India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitution_of_India "Constitution of India"), was sent to China in 1957 on a Government of India fellowship to establish a direct cross-cultural and inter-civilization bridge. Noted Indian scholar [Rahul Sankrityayan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rahul_Sankrityayan "Rahul Sankrityayan") and diplomat [Natwar Singh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Natwar_Singh "Natwar Singh") were also there, and [Sarvapalli Radhakrishnan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarvapalli_Radhakrishnan "Sarvapalli Radhakrishnan") paid a visit to the PRC.

# Lens 1B.8 — Xi Jinping (China), 2023

**Question:** In crisis moments, did the ruler de-escalate, communicate clearly, and preserve channels that reduce accidental war?

**One-sentence answer for 2023:** The 2023 record is **mostly positive on the visible crisis-management dimension** (no active shooting wars involving China; a renewed in-person Biden–Xi summit on 15 November 2023 that explicitly agreed to resume mil-to-mil communications; rhetorical restraint on personal nuclear threats; brokering of the Iran–Saudi rapprochement in March 2023) but **negative on the structural channel-preservation dimension** (no improvement to the 2022 cancellation of mil-to-mil communications until the November 2023 reset; active maintenance of crisis-amplifying operational pressure in the South China Sea, around Taiwan, and at the Line of Actual Control with India; continuation of a 2023 PLARF leadership purge that itself created a new crisis-management fragility).

---

## A. Claim-level findings — Xi de-escalated or preserved channels in 2023

### 1. Brokering of the Iran–Saudi rapprochement (March 2023)

- **Claim A1.** In March 2023, after months of Beijing-mediated talks, Iran and Saudi Arabia agreed to restore diplomatic relations, ending a seven-year rupture. This is a positive de-escalation act in a region where the two countries' rivalry has historically fueled proxy conflict and nuclear tensions. The China-brokered agreement was concluded on 10 March 2023.

## C. Net reading for lens 1B.8

The 2023 record is **mixed — positive on some dimensions, negative on others**:

- **Positive:** Iran–Saudi de-escalation; resumption of US-China mil-to-mil communications; Xi personal rhetorical restraint (NFU reaffirmed); no shooting wars involving China in 2023; retention of India bilateral architecture; no spiral to armed clash after the 10 November 2023 South China Sea confrontation.
- **Negative:** Sustained Taiwan Strait operational pressure (Fourth Taiwan Strait Crisis continued); sustained South China Sea grey-zone pressure against the Philippines; the PLARF leadership purge created a new fragility in the nuclear C2 chain; no upgrade to nuclear hotlines; no binding COC; PLARF social-media nuclear-strike normalization; no Taiwan crisis framework.

The **most consequential 2023 act** under this lens was the November 2023 mil-to-mil communications reset, which is real but narrow — it does not address the structural channels (nuclear hotline, cross-strait, Taiwan) where the most acute accidental-war risks live. The **most consequential failure** was the PLARF leadership purge, which placed non-nuclear-specialist replacements at the top of the nuclear C2 chain during a year of active conventional coercion against Taiwan and in the South China Sea.

**Net judgment: 1B.8 reads as mixed — Xi executed one real channel-preservation act (mil-to-mil) and one real de-escalation act (Iran–Saudi), but continued active crisis-amplifying operational pressure across multiple theaters and weakened the nuclear C2 chain that would have to manage any escalation. A strong ruler would have used the November 2023 summit as a platform for binding crisis-management frameworks, not just channel reactivation.**
